Another Pakistani national had sustained injuries. "Pakistan strongly condemns the Houthi attack on a non-combatant commercial vessel. Such attacks endanger innocent lives, constitute a violation of international law, and pose a serious threat to freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the safety of commercial shipping in the Red Sea," the minister said in a post on X. Pakistan's foreign Ministry was in contact with Saudi Arabia and Yemen to ascertain further details of the incident, Dar said. Meanwhile, the Pakistani Embassy in Riyadh was coordinating the retrieval and repatriation of the mortal remains of their deceased nationals. Vessels under attack amid Middle East conflict On Tuesday, the US and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis reported separate attacks on shipping as peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran seemingly stagnated once again. At the southern end of the Red Sea, a suspected Houthi attack on a small cargo vessel killed four crew members, Yemen's transport ministry had said. It was not immediately clear is this was the same vessel Dar was referring to. Commercial shipping and seafarers passing through the Middle East have increasingly come under attack by both the US and Iran since the conflict began earlier this year. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw. Photograph: George Marciniw via Facebook View image in fullscreen Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw. Photograph: George Marciniw via Facebook Los Angeles TV reporter and pilot who died in Los Angeles helicopter crash were covering a story NBC4 colleagues Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw were working to report on a collision between a bus and an SUV Anna Betts and Uwa Ede-Osifo Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.59 EDT First published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 10.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More details are emerging after a local news helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighborhood on Tuesday evening, killing two people onboard and one person on the ground. Eliana Moreno, an aerial photojournalist, and pilot George Marciniw have been identified as the two victims on the helicopter. A third individual, Edy Gutierrez Mejia, a pedestrian near the crash site, was also killed. Authorities said the helicopter crashed in the Chatsworth area, in the San Fernando valley, at around 7pm local time, while it was covering another deadly crash involving a metro bus and an SUV. An SUV collided into the bus around 5pm local time, killing two people and sending multiple others to a hospital. The helicopter came down around two hours later, killing three people, officials said, and multiple people were also brought to a hospital. The SUV’s driver, 36-year-old Bailee Lynn Rios, has been arrested on suspicion of murder, according to several news reports. The helicopter was reporting for NBC4, the local NBC affiliate, the station announced on Tuesday evening. During a later broadcast, Colleen Williams, an NBC4 Los Angeles news anchor, confirmed live on air that two of the station’s colleagues were onboard the helicopter and were killed in the crash. Williams identified them as Moreno and Marciniw. 0:52 Los Angeles news anchor confirms station’s deadly helicopter crash while on air – video “We’re coming on the air with heavy hearts tonight because we lost valued friends and colleagues just before 7pm,” Williams said. “News Chopper 4 crashed in Chatsworth while on assignment tonight. Both people onboard and a third person on the ground were killed. Our crew was there covering a deadly crash involving a bus and an SUV just a couple of blocks away.” The anchors said that Moreno was born and raised in Orange county and graduated from Chapman University with a degree in broadcast journalism and political science. Marciniw grew up in southern California and graduated from Burbank high school in 1974. The two began flying together in 2023. The station’s first story of the evening was “supposed to be with News Chopper 4” but that “all of a sudden, we lost contact with the chopper”, the anchors said. NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52 issued a joint statement expressing condolences: “We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.” At a news conference on Tuesday night, Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, said that it was a “very, very, very tragic day” for the city. “We lost five Angelenos today,” Bass said. “And my heart certainly go out to the family and friends of all of those that we lost. This is a heartbreaking night for our city and my thoughts and prayers are first and foremost with the families and loved ones that we lost today. Our hearts are with those impacted by the bus collision and the helicopter crash, and with the entire community who lost members of their team while they were doing their job.” The cause of the crash remains unknown, as National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration launch an investigation. Several experts, however, have speculated that an engine failure downed the aircraft. “It just has all the earmarks of a potential loss of engine power and a dangerous decrease in the main rotor speed,” Jeff Guzzetti, an aviation safety expert, told the Associated Press. Zoey Tur, a longtime LA news helicopter journalist, also hypothesized engine failure was the cause. Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, released a statement on Tuesday night on the incident, saying that “our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family”. “Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight,” he added. https://www.politico.eu/article/liberal-.text: BRIGHTON, England — The Liberal Democrats want to defeat Nigel Farage — just don’t mention working with Labour to do it. The third-largest party in Westminster has made opposing Reform UK central to its annual conference by the English coast this week. Yet what that actually might entail has been conspicuously absent from the discussion in Brighton. Neither Andy Burnham’s ruling Labour Party or Farage’s right-wing force — currently a close first and second in opinion polls — is on course to win a majority at the next general election, due by August 2029. It means both could be looking for a coalition partner. Advertisement Advertisement Lib Dem leader Ed Davey — who addresses the party faithful Tuesday — told ITV News on Monday he believes there is likely to be a hung parliament next time around. And he has already talked up the threat of a right-wing pact, warning that Farage and Conservative boss Kemi Badenoch could turn Britain into a “Trump-satellite state” — despite both of their repeated protestations that this isn’t on the cards. An “orange wall” of Lib Dem MPs “will not let [Farage and Badenoch] pass,” Davey has said. The subtext is that the Lib Dems will do whatever it takes to keep Reform’s hands off power — and in the U.K.’s first-past-the-post electoral system, that would most likely mean propping up a minority Labour administration. “Labour is open to working with us,” claimed one Lib Dem MP, citing Burnham and Davey’s collegiate relationship at prime minister’s questions and work on social care, though they were coy about whether that means in a future formal coalition when pushed. At least five other Lib Dems MPs POLITICO spoke with were also reluctant to discuss the prospect of a coalition with Labour. And while the Lib Dems are keen to show they would like to be in government again, it seems they would rather leave the realities of how they get there below the radar for now. Advertisement Advertisement Scars on their back Mention of a coalition often sparks fear into the heart of a Lib Dem because of how the last one ended. “We got hammered in 2015,” a second Lib Dem MP said, recalling how the party crashed from 57 Westminster seats to just eight after five years as junior partner in the Tory-Lib Dem government. Though many Lib Dems will defend that government’s record, the 2015 thrashing means MPs would be cautious about jumping into a coalition again. “I always feel a bit icky when thinking [about coalition deals], because it’s not up to us,” said a third MP. “It’s up to the voters who end up with the numbers for those sorts of things to work.” Ed Davey talks with Keir Starmer in Westminster Abbey on May 6, 2023. | Pool photo by Richard Pohle via WPA/Getty Images The last coalition “did us a lot of damage for doing the right thing,” said a fourth MP. The party faced a huge backlash over its U-turn on increasing tuition fees, and its support for massive government spending cuts. Lib Dems are aware they would have to consider the compromises their activists — as well as voters — would accept as a price for power. Advertisement Advertisement A fifth MP called for the party to have three really clear policies identifiable in their manifesto that would serve as “red lines” going into any negotiations, warning “otherwise we go in with a weak hand.” One alternative — if Labour fell short of an overall majority — would be for the Lib Dems to enter a confidence and supply arrangement, where they would remain outside government, but influence government policy in return for supporting the government in budgets and votes of confidence. Clear red water MPs believe there is peril for the party in being seen to be preparing for Labour tie-up — particularly when many of their voters used to be Conservatives. In 2024, the Lib Dems made gains in rural constituencies where former Conservative voters wanted to see the back of a Tory government they had once supported — and the party continues to target Conservatives voters disillusioned by Badenoch’s shift to the right. Davey has been careful not to rule out a future pact with the Tories — keeping his fire closely trained on Farage. But some Lib Dem MPs are beginning to think a more combative approach to Labour is needed. “The constructive opposition approach went on for far too long [under Keir Starmer],” said a sixth MP in a formerly Tory seat, who thinks the same thing is happening with Burnham who they claim has “no substance.” Advertisement Advertisement That MP suggested the more emollient approach should cut both ways, and “when a Tory frontbencher says something sensible, we should work with them.” The Tories are leaping on Davey’s stance, branding the Lib Dems “Labour enablers” who are failing to hold the government to account. A seventh Lib Dem MP said they believe the party shouldn’t rule out working with the Tories — if they return to more moderate roots. A Liberal Democrat spokesperson said: “The chances of a hung parliament are greater than ever, and in that scenario, experience counts.” Cut through Beyond the coalition talk, Davey is facing bigger questions about whether his party is cutting through at a time when U.K. politics is in flux. “We’re not populist. We’re not going to say things for clicks,” the first MP quoted said, while admitting: “I’m not going to pretend there aren’t frustrations” about the party being heard more loudly and clearly. Advertisement Advertisement The fifth MP quoted above agrees. There’s a frustration around the messaging being “all about who we’re against” rather than “standing up for our values” as the antithesis of Reform, they said. An eighth MP said they are concerned the repeated references to Reform could work against them because “naming those you want to do down doesn’t work, it does the opposite.” It frames Farage in voters’ minds and risks a self-fulfilling prophecy that fuels his success, they said. It is against this backdrop that questions have loomed at the Lib Dem gathering about whether Davey really is the right person to take on Farage and Burnham. Trouble at the top Julian Brazil, the Lib Dem leader of Devon County Council, told the BBC that “all the evidence” suggests Davey, who has led the party for six years, is no longer the right man for the job. Most of the MPs Playbook spoke to for this piece did not want to discuss defenestrating their leader — at least not publicly. Nigel Farage during day two of the Reform UK party conference at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham, on Sept. 5, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Yet plenty of delegates are asking fairly existential questions about what the party stands for in the new era of a Burnham led-government in debates on the conference floor. Advertisement Research published by More in Common has done little to improve the mood. Polling by the think tank found fewer people understand what the Lib Dems stand for than Restore — the hard-right party founded only a few months ago by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. Asked to describe Davey, the two most common responses were “don’t know” and “not sure.” The fifth MP quoted above warned there is a disconnect between the leadership and the activist base. Those around Davey are “shocked” when confronted with how unpopular he is among some members, they said. Davey’s told the Sunday Times’ he “shares” his critics’ frustration — but blamed the party’s lack of progress on the “crazy politics we’re in.” The Lib Dem spokesperson quoted above insists the party is in an “incredibly strong position” and has seen its “best result for a century, and achieved a record breaking streak of remarkable local election results” under Davey’s leadership. Bobby Dean, the Lib Dems’ shadow commons leader, told POLITICO: “Ed has all the ingredients to be a really powerful messenger.” He points to sections in the More in Common polling that shows among respondents who did know Davey, he was described as “likable” and “competent.” “Those are like good building blocks to start from,” Dean says. The problem for Davey is that, six years into the job, plenty in his party are starting to wonder how much longer the building work can go on. Advertisement

https://www.eurasiareview.com/23092026-f.text: One of the fragments of the sixth-century manuscript venerated as a relic, attributed to the authorship of the Evangelist St. Mark. | Credit: Courtesy of Tseng Kuang Yi Religion 1 Europe September 23, 2026 EWTN News 0 Comments By EWTN News By Victoria Cardiel Key Takeaways: For the first time in about 700 years, Aquileia has reunited three pieces of a sixth-century uncial Gospel book (Codex Forojuliensis / Cividale) long venerated as if St. Mark had written it; tradition holds Mark founded Aquileia’s church, later an apostolic patriarchate. Likely made in Ravenna and in Aquileia by the late 800s (Patriarch Theodemar), Mark’s seven quires were split off in the 12th–13th centuries, given a silver-gilt cover, and treated as a relic. Charles IV took two quires to Prague in 1354; Venice seized the rest after 1420. Humidity ruined much of the Venetian share. Before the split the book was a Liber Vitae with 1,500-plus names (Louis II, Engelberga, Svatopluk, Bulgarian envoys). The show “Seven Centuries. Three Fragments. One European Story” runs to April 2027; originals are out only the first six weeks, then facsimiles. For the first time in seven centuries, Aquileia, a city in northeastern Italy with a fascinating past, has reunited the three scattered fragments of a sixth-century manuscript that for centuries was venerated as if it were the Gospel written by St. Markʼs own hand. The author of the Gospel that bears his name was St. Peter’s interpreter and secretary. He followed the apostle to Rome, where he witnessed his preaching in the homes of the first followers of Christ, who dared to defy the Roman Empire’s laws governing worship. St. Mark carefully recorded every courageous word of that early catechesis, and his notes became a firsthand source for the story of Jesus’ life. Today, Aquileia, a small town of just over 3,000 inhabitants, treasures St. Mark’s memory as the founder of one of the most flourishing Christian communities of the Middle Ages. After the Edict of Milan in A.D. 313, the city, situated at the crossroads of East and West and serving as a bridge between the Mediterranean world and Slavic culture, became a center for the spread of Christianity into Central Europe and the Balkans. By the fifth century, it had even been honored with the title of apostolic city, and its bishop held the rank of patriarch. That privilege was reserved only for dioceses that traced their origins to the preaching of an apostle. “We preserve extraordinary medieval frescoes in the basilica depicting St. Mark arriving here to found the city’s first Christian community. That is why we believe he truly came to Aquileia,” Aquileia tour guide Anna Sairu told “EWTN Noticias,” the Spanish-language broadcast edition of EWTN News. The codex that became a relic One of the principal witnesses to this tradition is the “Codex Forojuliensis,” also known as the “Cividale Gospel Book.” The sixth-century manuscript, written in uncial script, the calligraphy reserved for sacred texts, originally contained all four Gospels in St. Jerome’s Latin translation. Scholars believe it was most likely produced in Ravenna, Italy. From there it arrived in Aquileia during the second half of the ninth century, where it was authenticated by the signature of Theodemar, patriarch of Aquileia. The presence of the codex strengthened the tradition linking St. Mark to the evangelization of the region. Its significance became so great that in 827 the Synod of Mantua recognized Aquileia’s ecclesiastical supremacy over Grado. Venice looked with suspicion on the growing religious prestige of its neighbor. Just a year later, in 828, Venetian merchants brought the relics attributed to the evangelist from Alexandria to the city on the lagoon. In doing so, “The Most Serene Republic” of Venice gained a patron of apostolic rank and strengthened the religious and political foundations of its power. The fragmented Gospel Between the 12th and 13th centuries, the seven quires — folded sheets of paper stitched into booklets — containing the Gospel of Mark were separated from the rest of the codex, rebound independently, and covered with an elaborate gilded silver binding that transformed the book into an object of veneration resembling a reliquary. From that point on, the manuscript ceased to be viewed as merely an ancient copy and began to be regarded as an autograph written by St. Mark himself. Medieval inventories of the Patriarchal Treasury of Aquileia reflect this belief. “The Gospel was fragmented when it was removed from the Gospel book containing all four Gospels and began to be regarded as an autograph of the evangelist himself. This is connected to the tradition that St. Mark evangelized this region of Italy, Aquileia, and its surrounding territory. During the 12th and 13th centuries, the Gospel of Mark acquired a life of its own and came to be regarded as an extraordinary relic,” Cristiano Tiussi, director of the Aquileia Foundation and curator of the exhibition, told “EWTN Noticias.” The emperor who wanted a piece of St. Mark The fame of the supposed authentic Gospel of St. Mark quickly spread across Europe. In 1354, while traveling to Rome to receive the imperial crown, Charles IV of Luxembourg stopped in Aquileia. At the time, his half-brother, Nicholas of Luxembourg, served as patriarch there. The emperor requested part of the revered manuscript and received two of the seven quires that comprised the Gospel of Mark. Those pages were taken to Prague, where they were deposited in St. Vitus Cathedral alongside the relics of St. Wenceslaus. Over the centuries, they became the oldest written document preserved in Czech libraries. The exhibition even displays the original documents recording Charles IV’s request to the patriarch of Aquileia. “Possessing part of the Gospel of St. Mark meant owning not only a religious relic but also a symbol of prestige, legitimacy, and power,” Tiussi noted. The conquest of Venice The remainder of the manuscript remained in Aquileia until May 30, 1420, when Doge Tommaso Mocenigo conquered the city. Venice then claimed the remaining fragments, arguing that they belonged beside the evangelist’s tomb in the Basilica of St. Mark. Their transfer symbolized Aquileia’s definitive incorporation into the Venetian sphere. The gesture also carried an unmistakable political significance. If Venice had claimed custody of the evangelist’s body since 828, it now also acquired part of the manuscript believed by tradition to have been written by his hand. As a result, the Gospel of Mark became permanently divided among the cities of Cividale del Friuli, Venice, and Prague. For the manuscript itself, however, the consequences proved devastating. Humidity from the Venetian lagoon gradually damaged the pages until they became almost illegible. Today, those remnants are preserved in a reliquary display case within the Treasury of St. Mark. A medieval Facebook The exhibition offers visitors a second surprise. Before it was dismantled, the manuscript served as a “Liber Vitae,” or “Book of the Living.” More than 1,500 names were entered into its pages by people who wished to be remembered in the prayers of the monastic community that safeguarded the codex. “This is one of the features that makes this Gospel book exceptional. In Italy, we know of only two Carolingian-era ‘libri vitae.’ This is one of them. These inscriptions, written in a hand different from the original uncial script, were initially simple liturgical annotations. They are notes written on the Gospel between the seventh and eighth centuries indicating which passages should be read during particular periods of the year or providing other instructions for the book’s liturgical use,” said Luca Villa, another curator of the exhibition. Beginning in the second half of the ninth century, the names of benefactors, nobles, pilgrims, and distinguished visitors were added. Among them were figures as notable as Emperor Louis II the Younger and his wife Engelberga, the Moravian prince Svatopluk, and envoys from the newly Christianized Kingdom of Bulgaria. “There are more than 1,500 important figures who wrote their names in the Gospel, not merely to leave a record of themselves but because they believed that by doing so they would share in the liturgical celebrations every time the book was used in the church where it was kept,” Villa told “EWTN Noticias.” For historians, these lists provide an extraordinary window into medieval Europe. They reveal a network of contacts, pilgrimages, and cultural exchanges linking distant regions centuries before the emergence of modern nation-states. A European story Now, for the first time in roughly 700 years, the three surviving portions of the Gospel have been reunited. The quires preserved in Prague have left the Czech Republic for the first time. The fragments kept in Venice have temporarily departed St. Mark’s Basilica. Together with the pages preserved in Friuli, they reconstruct a story that had remained fragmented since the Middle Ages. Czech curator Martina Dlabajová said she believes the reunion also symbolizes the very essence of Europe. “What is beautiful is that, while acknowledging that each fragment has had a different history and followed a different path, by bringing them together we have chosen to embrace that shared history. That is why the exhibition’s title speaks of ‘Seven Centuries, Three Fragments, One European Story,’ because the three fragments never ceased to be part of a common narrative, and that narrative is a European one,” she explained. “I also like to emphasize that Europe itself should recognize differences, accept that distinct histories exist, and understand that those different histories from various countries enrich our shared history,” she added in comments to “EWTN Noticias.” The exhibition, “The Gospel of Mark: Seven Centuries . Three Fragments. One European Story,” will remain open through April 2027. Due to the fragility of the parchment, however, restrictions are necessary. The original manuscripts will be on display only during the exhibition’s first six weeks. They will then be replaced by high-resolution digital reproductions. https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/10/27/cypru.text: Road deaths in Cyprus rose by 10 per cent in 2025, with 45 fatalities recorded, according to figures published on Tuesday by the European Commission’s transport directorate. The island’s road fatality rate was slightly above the EU average of 43 deaths per million inhabitants, although the number of fatalities remained 13 per cent below the 2019 level and 12 per cent below the 2017 figure. Data for the first half of this year show a fall of more than 10 per cent compared with the same period last year. However, Cyprus has recorded 34 road fatalities so far this year, matching the number registered at the same point in 2025, which was the deadliest year of the past five years. Fourteen of this year’s victims were motorcyclists. Speeding and mobile phone use remain among the main contributing factors in fatal collisions, while drivers under the age of 24 feature prominently among those killed. A European transport safety council report published in June found Cyprus cut road deaths by 13.5 per cent between 2019 and 2025 and by 21.1 per cent over the past decade, slightly better than the EU average of 20.2 per cent. Across the EU, 19,350 people died in road collisions in 2025, a decrease of 3 per cent compared with 2024 and 15 per cent compared with 2019. Only Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, Poland and Romania are currently on track to meet the EU target of halving road deaths by 2030. Bulgaria recorded the highest road fatality rate, at 71 deaths per million inhabitants, followed by Romania with 68 and Croatia with 65. Sweden recorded the lowest rate, at 19 deaths per million inhabitants.
